tip: In the plural after 'die', all adjectives end in '-en': 'die warmen bunten Herbstfarben'.
When something other than the subject opens the sentence, the verb stays second: 'Wegen des Staus kommen wir zu spät'.
In a passive with a modal, 'werden' goes to the very end after the participle: 'müssen geschützt werden'.
Many one-syllable adjectives add an umlaut in the superlative: 'klug' becomes 'die klügste'.
Weather verbs need the dummy subject 'es': 'es werde morgen schneien', never 'schneien' on its own.
The dative plural normally adds '-n' to the noun itself: 'mit frischen Kräutern' (from 'Kräuter').
Because 'warten auf' takes the accusative, the relative word is 'auf den', not 'auf dem': 'der Zug, auf den wir warten'.
Than in a comparison is 'als', not 'wie': 'Obst ist gesünder als Süßigkeiten' (fruit is healthier than sweets).
In a modal passive the modal stays in second position and 'werden' goes last: 'Hier darf nicht geraucht werden' (smoking is not allowed here).
'Lieber' is the comparative of 'gern' and marks what you prefer: 'er fährt lieber Fahrrad' (he would rather cycle).
A superlative before a noun keeps the article and takes an ending: 'der schönste Urlaub' (the most beautiful holiday).
In the passive perfect, 'werden' becomes 'worden', not 'geworden': 'zugestellt worden' (was delivered).
'Innerhalb' takes the genitive: 'innerhalb eines Jahres' (within a year).
'Trotz' takes the genitive: 'trotz des Gewitters' (despite the thunderstorm).
'Wegen' takes the genitive in careful German: 'wegen der Dürre' (because of the drought); everyday speech often uses the dative.
A passive with no named doer uses 'wird' plus the past participle: 'In Deutschland wird viel Brot gegessen' (a lot of bread is eaten).
A passive with no real subject can open with the placeholder 'es': 'es wird darum gebeten' (it is requested).
'Ungeachtet' is a formal preposition with the genitive: 'ungeachtet der Kritik' (regardless of the criticism).
'Unterhalb' is a spatial preposition with the genitive: 'unterhalb der Brücke' (below the bridge).
Start the sentence with 'deshalb' and the verb jumps ahead of the subject: 'deshalb sollten alle Teilnehmer' (therefore all participants should).
A relative clause sits after a comma and sends its verb to the end: 'das Haus, das mein Großvater gebaut hat'.
'Gut' is irregular in the superlative: 'gut', 'besser', 'am besten'. The bread here 'schmeckt am besten' (tastes the best).
Add '-s' to a lowercased day for a habit: 'freitags' means every Friday, not one specific Friday.
'Beitreten' takes a dative object, so its relative pronoun is 'dem': 'der Verein, dem mein Sohn beigetreten ist'.
When a relative clause needs a preposition, it goes first: 'die Firma, bei der meine Schwester arbeitet'.
The doer in a passive is marked with 'von', here fused into 'vom' ('von' + 'dem'): 'wurden vom Arbeitgeber abgelehnt' (were rejected by the employer).
After 'nichts', 'etwas' or 'alles' the relative pronoun is 'was', not 'das': 'nichts, was ihn von seinem Ziel abbringen könnte'.
As a conjunction 'während' means while and sends the verb to the end: 'während meine Frau arbeitet' (while my wife works).
'Seitdem' opens a time clause and pushes the verb to the end: 'seitdem er regelmäßig trainiert' (since he trains regularly).
'Mangels' is a formal preposition with the genitive, common in legal language: 'mangels ausreichender Beweise' (for lack of sufficient evidence).
